fields.sample_size: two informal communities in Xochimilco (Tiziclipa, about 364 houses; San Jose Obrero, about 150 houses); 21 household questionnaire respondents per community (42 in all, snowball sampling along water-truck delivery sites) plus semi-structured interviews with delivery-site leaders, water-truck drivers and local authorities
fields.study_design: comparative qualitative case study of two informal communities (household questionnaire and semi-structured interviews)
fields.effect_estimate: In the community with stable leadership and strong collective agency, self-organisation produced more efficient public water-truck delivery and low consumption from private sellers; in the other, weak leadership and self-organisation pushed residents to individual action (buying more private water) instead of collectively securing public supply. Residents of informal settlements cannot legally demand water; the study argues for formally recognising and compensating collective agency. Qualitative comparison, no effect estimate.
fields.section: Full text: Abstract; 4.1 case communities; 4.2 data collection and analysis; 5 Results; 6 Discussion

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a comparative case study of two informal communities in Xochimilco, Mexico City (21 questionnaire respondents each, plus leader, driver and official interviews) found that stable community leadership and collective agency made public water-truck delivery more efficient and reduced reliance on private sellers; qualitative, read in full text 2026-10-04.
pdf_note: International Journal of the Commons 2023 article (Drive file RB877CA5A448E), HTML-converted text of about 69,000 characters; the results section was only skimmed
notes: The first extraction had no sample and described the access problem generally; the full text gives the two communities, 21 respondents each, and the contrast in collective agency. Informal tenure status is the legal-status mechanism (residents cannot legally demand water).
